dek: Halloween, the time change, and why adults mask up as the year turns dark.

slides.label: The Hour
slides.text: This year Halloween got an extra hour: clocks fell back at 2 a.m., so 1 to 2 a.m. happened *twice*.

slides.label: Ancient Roots
slides.text: Halloween traces back nearly *2,000 years* to Samhain, when the Celts believed the dead crossed into the living world.

slides.label: Soul Cakes
slides.text: Medieval beggars prayed for the dead in exchange for *soul cakes*, a custom Irish immigrants turned into trick-or-treating.

slides.label: Latin America
slides.text: Across Latin America, Nov. 1 honors the *angelitos* who died young, and Nov. 2 belongs to the adults.

slides.label: Worldwide
slides.text: Haiti's *Fèt Gede*, Guatemala's giant kites and Bolivia's decorated skulls all keep the same week for the dead.

slides.label: The Cost
slides.text: A Danish study found an *11% jump* in new depression diagnoses right after the clocks fall back each November.

slides.label: Adults Take Over
slides.text: In 2026, adults spent *more on costumes* than on their kids', a shift born in queer Halloween balls in the Castro and NYC's Village Parade.

slides.label: What's Underneath
slides.text: Long before stores sold skeleton suits, people across the islands were already *painting their faces* for the dead.

question: Which do you celebrate: Halloween, Día de Muertos, or both?

caption_instagram:
This Halloween, one hour happened twice: when daylight saving time ended on November 1, the clock fell back exactly as the veil between worlds was supposed to thin.

Samhain gave us the dead walking close. The Church gave us All Saints and All Souls. Irish immigrants gave us soul cakes turned into trick-or-treat. Across Latin America, the Caribbean and beyond, families never stopped keeping that week for their ancestors, from Día de los Muertos altars to Haiti's Fèt Gede to Bolivia's painted skulls.

Somewhere along the way, grown adults took the night back too, turning it into billions in costume spending, with roots in queer community balls in the Castro and Greenwich Village.

Which do you celebrate: Halloween, Día de Muertos, or both?

caption_linkedin:
A kids' puppet procession in 1974 Greenwich Village grew into the largest Halloween parade in the world. It didn't start as a mass market play. It started because a community needed a night to be fully itself.

That's the quiet lesson inside this story about Halloween, Día de Muertos, and the week the dead come home. Queer communities in the Castro and the Village built adult Halloween first. Retail followed decades later. In 2026, American adults spent more on their own costumes than on their kids'.

Culture gets built by the people who need it most. Everyone else asks to come in after.

Which do you celebrate: Halloween, Día de Muertos, or both?
